Unofficial until approved by the

  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  May 24, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:07 p.m., on Monday, May 24, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met in Council
Chambers.

PRESENT:  LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present physically, via teleconference, and via video conference: City Manager
Binnquist, City Attorney Montes, Assistant City Manager Garcia, City Clerk Myles, Director of
Finance Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias,
Director of Library LohGuan, Marketing and Communications Specialist Nguyen, Director of
Community Development Ho, Deputy Director of Community Development Reynoso, Fire Chief
Phelps, Police Chief Parra, Director of Human Resources Ko

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Pérez

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-65

The City Clerk hereby reports that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City
Council being held this evening pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section
54955 and 54956 of the Government Code of the State of California.

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES
Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council
taking action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may
determine that the title has been read.

Action Taken:  On motion of Ms. LEE, seconded by Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, the City
Council determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public agenda had
been read, and waived further reading. Hearing no objections, the Mayor so ordered.

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

CEREMONIALS

1.  A.  REORGANIZATION: ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL – F2M21-46

  In accordance with Alhambra City Charter Sec. 29, this was the time for
  the rotation of the Mayor and Vice Mayor. Accordingly, Vice Mayor

  Mayor, respectively.

  REMARKS, RECOGNITIONS and ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
  by outgoing
  MAYOR SASHA RENÉE PÉREZ

  Public Comment:
  The following people thanked Mayor Pérez for her successful term as mayor and

  2) Maggie Clark, Councilmember of Rosemead
  3) Yvonne Yu, Mayor of Monterey Park
  4) Cindy Lee, representing Congresswoman Judy Chu
  5) Henry Lo, Mayor Pro-Tem of Monterey Park and representing Senator Ed Chau
  6) Nicolas Kiet Quach, a student at Alhambra High School, President of the Youth
  Commission, and an intern for Ms. Pérez
  7) Sandra Armenta, Councilmember of Rosemead
  8) Representing Los Angeles County Supervisor Katherine Barger

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and MAZA each offered warm
  regards to their fellow Councilmembers and their accomplishments, thanked Mayor
  Pérez for her successful term as mayor and offered best wishes to Incoming Mayor Lee
  and Vice Mayor Maloney.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:
  The following people thanked Mayor Pérez for her successful term as mayor and
  offered best wishes to Incoming Mayor Lee and Vice Mayor Maloney:

  1) Cliff Bender
  2) Sean McMorris
  3) Lewis McCammon

  to incoming
  VICE MAYOR JEFF MALONEY
  Councilperson of the Third District
  and to incoming
  MAYOR KATHERINE LEE
  Councilperson of the First District

  REMARKS, RECOGNITIONS and ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
  by
  MAYOR LEE & VICE MAYOR MALONEY

2.  COMMENDATIONS: CHINATOWN SERVICE CENTER AND HERALD CHRISTIAN
  HEALTH CENTER – F2M21-3

  Mayor Lee and the Alhambra City Council wished to recognize and thank Chinatown
  Service Center and Herald Christian Health Center for their partnership, hard work
  and collaboration in the fast, efficient and safe administration of the COVID-19 vaccine
  to those in need. Chinatown Service Center hosted a vaccination site at the Alhambra
  Civic Center Library on April 20, 2021 and administered vaccinations to 273 people.
  Hearld Christian Health Center ensured Alhambra residents and interested members of
  the public were vaccinated by hosting a vaccination site on April 23 and April 26, 2021.
  The City of Alhambra deeply appreciates the efforts of the management and staff of
  Chinatown Service Center and Herald Christian Health Center who ensured Alhambra
  residents and other members of the public were provided protection against the COVID-
  19 virus. The City of Alhambra was grateful for the efforts of Chinatown Service Center
  and Herald Christian Health Center to promote the health and well-being of our
  community.

PUBLIC HEARING

3.  PUBLIC WORKS MAINTENANCE & IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT & POLICE
  FACILITIES ASSESSMENT DISTRICT: FISCAL YEAR 2021-2022 RENEWALS –
  F2M21-45, N2M21-62, R2M21-21, R2M21-22

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M21-62 for the City Council to hold a
  public hearing to consider the following:

  A.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone A includes
  the downtown area only and was established to provide a source of funding to
  operate and maintain specialized improvements in the downtown area. Those
  improvements included items such as decorative sidewalk planters, landscape
  medians, decorative sidewalk and paving and the Washington Twin streetlights.
  This assessment was proposed to be unchanged from the 2020-21 level; and,

  B.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone B was
  established to fund debt service on a bond issue and ongoing maintenance and
  3
5-24-21
   operation of the City-wide street lights, sidewalks, curb and gutters, streets,
  street trees, median landscaping and municipal parking lots and structures. The
  work would be performed by a combination of a concrete crew, a two-person
  electrical crew (who also maintain traffic signals), an asphalt crew, and
  contractors. This assessment was proposed to be unchanged from the 2020-21
  level; and,

  C.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone C was
  established in 1987 and includes generally those properties located on both
  sides of Main Street, between Atlantic and Palm, and on both sides of Palm,
  between Main and Commonwealth. The purpose of Zone C was to provide
  funding for the ongoing maintenance and operation of the public improvements,
  which were constructed in the Auto Row area and included the grass parkway,
  the feature lights between Atlantic and Olive, and the street trees. This
  assessment was proposed to be unchanged from the 2020-21 level; and,

  D.  The Alhambra Police Facilities Assessment District (PFAD) assessment was
  created in 1991 by the City Council after a vote in which nearly 60 percent of the
  voters indicated approval for the proposal. The assessment paid the debt service
  on the bonds that were used to build the police facility. This assessment was
  proposed to be unchanged from the 2020-21 level, which for a single-family
  home is $59.56.

  Director of Public Works and Utilities RAY delivered a staff report on the item.

  Opened/Closed Public Hearing: Mayor LEE opened the public hearing; and, as
  there was no one present wishing to speak, she closed the same.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  The City Council, by one motion, adopted the following:

  1)  Resolution No. R2M21-21 entitled: A Resolution of the Alhambra City Council
  ordering the renewal of the City of Alhambra Public Works Maintenance and
  Improvements District No. 1 for Fiscal Year 2021-2022, confirming the
  Assessment Diagram and Assessment therefor and providing for the
  Assessment Levy in connection therewith; and,

  2)  Resolution No. R2M21-22 entitled: A Resolution of the Alhambra City Council
  ordering the renewal of the City of Alhambra Police Facilities Assessment District
  No. 91-1 for Fiscal Year 2021-2022, confirming the Assessment Diagram and
  Assessment therefor and providing for the Assessment Levy in connection
  therewith
  Vote:  Moved:  MAZA  Seconded:  PÉREZ
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ, MALONEY, MAZA, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

PRESENTATIONS

4.  UPDATE FROM SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA EDISON – F2M21-16
  4
5-24-21
   Director of Public Works and Utilities RAY introduced Jeannette SORIANO, Government
  Relations Manager from Southern California Edison (SCE) who provided an overview of
  how SCE is working to increase system capacity and reliability. Ray POLK, Local Public
  Affairs Manager, also contributed to the presentation regarding the vegetation
  management and tree removal program. Brian Howard, District Manager for the
  Montebello District, and Edward Vega, Operations Supervisor for the Montebello District,
  were also present for comments. The presentation is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER, Ms. SORIANO discussed the
  capital improvements plan and the estimated dates for completion. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER and Ms. SORIANO next discussed the rolling blackouts and SCE’s work with
  the Department of Social Services to maintain emergency power for the senior citizen
  community via generators.

  Mayor LEE discussed her work with SCE to provide compensation to residents that
  experienced food loss due to repeated power outages. She expressed concerns and
  discussed equipment management and maintenance, stressing the need to replace
  equipment before residents experience outages. Ms. SORIANO discussed the
  maintenance process. Ms. LEE also discussed the capital improvements projects
  including the Circuit Rebuild Program and the Circuit Reliability Upgrade with Ms.
  SORIANO and Mr. VEGA.

  Action Taken:  City Council received the informational report.

5.  CGI COMMUNICATIONS STREET BANNER PROGRAM OPPORTUNITY – F2M21-16

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a brief overview of the City’s current banner policy and
  clarified that depending on Council’s decision, the policy may have to be updated in
  accordance with recent caselaw. Marketing and Communications Specialist NGUYEN
  delivered a staff report. In 2019, the City partnered with CGI Communications for the
  Love My City Video Program to encourage civic engagement and develop a stronger
  sense of community trust. Recently, CGI Communications approached Alhambra staff
  with another marketing opportunity within the City—this time, in the form of a street
  banner program with CGI. Under the proposed program, the City would engage in a
  multi-year contract to showcase banners across town featuring Alhambra’s businesses
  and business logos. The banners would also feature a decorative design of the City’s
  choosing. CGI has a Graphic Arts Department to assist the City with design and
  concept. Ms. Nguyen presented additional features of this potential banner program,
  delivered a presentation which is on file in the City Clerk’s office, and sought direction
  from the City Council on Alhambra participating in CGI Communication’s Street Banner
  Program. Nikki CARROLL, representing CGI Communications, was available for
  comment.

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ discussed the banner policy and the types of
  banners that would be excluded, such as political content, with Ms. CARROLL and Mr.
  MONTES. Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mayor LEE requested more
  information regarding the details of the existing policy and requested that the discussion
  continue at another Council meeting. Councilmember MALONEY agreed that he would
  also prefer more information regarding what type of information could be excluded.
  5
5-24-21
   Action Taken:  City Council continued the item for further discussion at a future
  Council meeting.

6.  DRAFT BUDGET FOR FY 2021-2022 & CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PLAN FOR
  FISCAL YEARS 2021-2022 THROUGH 2025-2026 – F2M21-17

  Director of Finance LIEU delivered a staff report and presentation, which are on file in
  the City Clerk’s Office. Staff requested that the City Council review and discuss the Draft
  Annual Budget for the City of Alhambra, the Golf Course Clubhouse Corporation, the
  Alhambra Capital Improvements Corporation and the Alhambra Public Financing
  Corporation for fiscal year 2021-2022 and the Capital Improvement Plan for fiscal years
  2021-2022 through 2025-2026. The Annual Budget and Capital Improvement Plan would
  come back for final City Council consideration and adoption at the June 14, 2021
  meeting.

PÉREZ:  Councilmember Pérez left Council Chambers at 7:37 p.m. and returned at 7:40
p.m.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Ms. LIEU discussed the
  emergency operation reserve funds, the rolling stock equipment reserve, building repair
  reserve, and the self-insurance reserve as well as the possibility of adding to the reserve
  funds from any potential future surplus funds. They continued to discuss State of
  California reimbursement funds. Councilmember MALONEY and Councilmember MAZA
  discussed the potential allotment and uses of the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA)
  COVID Relief Funds with Ms. LIEU. Councilmember PÉREZ thanked staff for their work.
  Mayor LEE discussed various details of the draft budget and continued to discuss the
  ARPA COVID Relief Funds with Ms. LIEU. Ms. LEE requested a presentation providing
  an update on the City’s CALPERS liability fund.

  Action Taken:  City Council reviewed and discussed the 2021-2022 fiscal year
  Draft Budget and the Capital Improvements Plan for fiscal years 2021-2022 through
  2025-2026.

7.  DISCUSSION ON THE RESTRUCTURING OF THE YOUTH COMMISSION AND
  PLANNING COMMISSION – F2M21-36

  Deputy City Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report. On February 22, 2021, the City
  Council received public comment and a request from staff for further direction on the
  possible restructuring of the City’s boards, committees, and commissions pursuant to the
  Council’s Strategic Plan and the goals of enhancing communications between Council
  and the residents through the role of resident volunteers and creating a more efficient
  and effective approach to board/committee/commission business. The Council received
  information on the City’s ten commission groups, including their composition, purpose,
  and frequency of meetings. In addition, the Council heard comment regarding potential
  for overlap of work for select groups. In some instances, the original scope of the work
  as described in the Municipal Code is no longer applicable and/or is no longer in concert
  with what’s needed today. Following public comment and Council discussion of the
  matter, the Council directed this item return at a later date with staggered review.
  Following public comment and Council discussion of the matter, the Council directed this
  6
5-24-21
   item return at a later date with staggered review. On April 12, 2021, the Council
  addressed changes to the Transportation Commission and the Civil Service
  Commission. Thereafter, on April 26, 2021, the Council also reviewed the Library Board
  of Trustees, Parks and Recreation Commission, and the Arts and Cultural Events
  Committee. On May 10, 2021, Council also provided feedback regarding the Design
  Review Board, Environmental Committee and the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee.
  This evening, the focus was be on changes desired for the City’s Youth Commission and
  Planning Commission.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Nicolas  Kiet
  Quach, a student at Alhambra High School and the President of the Youth Commission,
  wrote regarding the merits of the Youth Commission and offered recommendations
  regarding Council’s comments and suggestions included in the report.

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ referred to Mr. Quach’s concerns regarding the
  lack of quorum in the Youth Commission, and requested that staff provide regular
  updates regarding the attendance to consider whether membership should be reduced
  in the future. She also requested that her fellow Councilmembers continue to monitor
  Commissioner attendance. She did not support changes to the age requirements to the
  commission. Councilmember MALONEY reversed his previous suggestion to disband
  the Youth Commission and providing alternate youth members on all other commissions
  and supported keeping the highly engaged Youth Commission. He suggested reducing
  the required number of commissioners to achieve a quorum rather than reducing the
  membership. Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER supported lowering the quorum
  number. Councilmember MAZA supported the Youth Commission as is and agreed with
  Ms. Pérez’s suggestion for Councilmembers to engage with their Commissioners. Ms.
  PÉREZ and City Attorney MONTES discussed the quorum requirements and suggested
  reducing the number to 5 Commissioners. Mayor LEE agreed that Council should
  engage with their Commissioners and discussed possible reasons for poor attendance
  to the Commission meetings. She recommended continued discussions with
  Commissioners regarding their additional commitments and their role in the commission.
  She supported reducing the commission to 10 members and suggested that the
  Commissioners set their own agenda, projects, and timeline for work which Council
  would approve. Ms. PÉREZ continued to discuss the Youth Summit, Ms. Lee’s
  suggestion, and fostering relationships within the commission.

  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested that no changes be made to the Planning
  Commission, discussed the requirements which list a preferred background in planning,
  and suggested additional training for commissioners. Mr. MALONEY agreed to make no
  changes at this time, but requested that Council continue to be open to reducing
  membership to five should a need arise. He agreed that there were advantages to
  having Commissioners with diverse backgrounds to provide different perspectives but
  agreed that those without professional backgrounds in Planning would benefit greatly
  from additional training. He requested prioritizing additional training and suggested
  seeking out options provided by the League of California Cities. Mr. MAZA and Ms.
  PÉREZ agreed with their fellow Councilmembers’ comments and suggestions. Ms.
  PÉREZ further suggested that the League of California Cities may have informational
  materials which could be provided to the City for the commissioners. She suggested
  modifying existing language regarding technical background requirements by stating that
  it was “highly recommended” in order to provide the expertise necessary for the Planning
  Commission while not hindering appointees with diverse perspectives. Ms. ANDRADE-
  7
5-24-21
   STADLER reflected that during her time on the Planning Commission, she found staff
  training as well as a joint meeting with City Council to be helpful as a guide in making
  decisions as a Commission. Mayor LEE agreed to keep the Planning Commission with
  ten members, that additional training would be beneficial, and that due to the nature of
  the Planning Commission which requires more time commitment, Commissioners should
  receive a stipend for their work.

  Mr. MONTES summarized Council’s suggestions for the Youth Commission wherein
  membership would remain at fifteen, quorum would continue to be set at five members,
  and that the Commission would be more active with the possibility of long-term projects.
  Regarding the Planning Commission, Council suggested retaining ten members,
  regularly scheduled technical training sessions, continued discussion regarding qualified
  elector status, and a joint meeting with Planning Commission and City Council. He
  clarified that there were no current technical or professional recommendations for the
  Planning Commission in the Alhambra Municipal Code. He stated that discussions
  regarding any stipend should continue in the context of all Commissioners. Ms. PÉREZ
  requested that there be suggested qualifications recommended for Planning
  Commissioners similar to that of the Design Review Board.

  Action Taken:  City Council provided direction on any structuring changes to the
  City’s Youth Commission and Planning Commission.

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 8 – 27)

All other items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of items #18 and #21, were
considered by the City Council to be routine and were enacted by one motion.

8.  NOTICE INVITING BIDS: SIXTH STREET SEWER MAIN REPLACEMENT PROJECT
  – F2M21-47, N2M21-66

  The Sewer Master Plan identified the Sixth Street sewer main between Front Street and
  San Marino Avenue as deficient in capacity and recommends replacement of the
  existing sewer main with a larger diameter sewer main. This project would replace
  approximately 1,400 feet of existing 10-inch sewer main to 12-inch sewer main. Plans
  and specifications were prepared; staff reviewed the plans and found them to be
  consistent with the City’s standards.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the distribution of a Notice Inviting Bids to
  qualified contractors for the 6th Street Sewer Main Replacement Project with bids due
  no later than 10:30 a.m. on June 17, 2021.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

  8
5-24-21
 9.  NOTICE INVITING BIDS: WATER MAIN REPLACEMENT PROJECT ON TERRACE
  AVENUE AND PYRENEES DRIVE – F2M21-48, N2M21-67

  The four-inch cast iron water mains on Terrace Avenue between Cabrillo Avenue and
  Pyrenees Drive and Pyrenees Drive between Cabrillo Avenue and Norwood Drive have
  had a history of breaks. Replacement of these water mains would greatly improve flow
  and enhance firefighting capabilities in an emergency. This project would replace the
  existing four-inch cast iron water mains with new 8-inch ductile iron water mains. The
  Project also included asphalt paving, replacing damaged sidewalk and curb and gutter,
  and installing new ADA ramps. Plans and specifications were prepared; staff reviewed
  the plans and found them to be consistent with City standards.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the distribution of a Notice Inviting Bids to
  qualified contractors for the Water Main Replacement Project on Terrace Avenue and
  Pyrenees Drive with bids due no later than 10:30 a.m. on June 10, 2021, and opened at
  11:00 a.m. that same day.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

10.  AUTHORIZE RFP: INSPECTION SERVICES FOR THE FY 2019-2020 SB1 STREET
  REHABILITATION PROJECT – F2M18-34, RFP2M21-12

  On April 26, 2021, the City Council approved the award of construction for the FY 2019-
  2020 SB 1 Street Rehabilitation Project. Staff requested approval of the distribution of a
  Request for Proposals for Professional Inspection Services for the Project.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of a Request for Proposals
  for Inspection Services for FY19-20 SB1 Street Rehabilitation Project with proposals due
  no later than 4:00 p.m. on June 17, 2021.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

11.  GRANT AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA AND THE SAN
  GABRIEL VALLEY MUNICIPAL WATER DISTRICT TO ASSIST RESIDENTS WITH
  PAYMENT OF DELIQUENT WATER BILLS – F2M21-49, C2M21-27, M2M21-58

  The San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District (SGVMWD) provides reliable
  supplemental water for the communities of Alhambra, Azusa, Monterey Park and Sierra
  Madre and procures water from the state water project used to supplement ground water
  9
5-24-21
   supplies among its four member cities. In response to the economic hardship that many
  residents of the Water District’s member cities have suffered due to the COVID-19
  pandemic, the Water District would provide the City with grant funds to the residents of
  Alhambra for the payment of delinquent account balances of water bills. Staff proposed
  guidelines for the administration of this program. Under the Alhambra Residential Utility
  Assistance Grant Program, financial assistance would be provided to low to moderate
  income residents with an emphasis on those negatively impacted by COVID-19. This
  program would offer a one-time grant up to $500 for payment of delinquent water bills on
  a first come, first serve basis. The Utilities Department staff would serve as the primary
  contact for implementation of the program. If approved, staff would market the program,
  accept and process applications, both in person and on-line, and reach out to past due
  eligible accounts.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved a Grant Agreement with the San Gabriel
  Valley Municipal Water District to receive $200,000 for payment assistance to the
  residents with delinquent water bills; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary
  to finalize Council’s action. (M2M21-58)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

12.  AWARD CONTRACT: PROFESSIONAL INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND
  SUPPORT SERVICES FOR THE POLCE DEPARTMENT – F2M21-34, RFP2M21-8,
  C2M21-28, M2M21-59

  On March 22, 2021, the City Council approved the distribution of a Request for
  Proposals (RFP) for Professional Information Technology and Support Services. There
  were six proposals received. Police staff reviewed and evaluated the proposals
  submitted and based on the requirements of the RFP, including expertise and public
  safety, qualifications, experience with similar projects, and cost, the proposal received
  from Scientia Consulting Group received the overall highest rating.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language
  approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, to Scientia Consulting Group to provide
  professional Information Technology and Support Services to the Police Department in
  an amount not to exceed $146,000 annually, commencing July 1, 2021 and terminating
  June 30, 2024, including two one-year extension periods; authorize the City Manager to
  execute the extensions, subject to satisfactory firm performance and future budget
  allocations; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s
  action. (M2M21-59)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  10
5-24-21
   Absent:  NONE

13.  AWARD CONTRACT: PURCHASE OF ONE 7-YARD DUMP TRUCK - F2M21-6A,
  N2M21-44, C2M21-29, M2M21-60

  On April 12, 2021, the City Council approved the distribution of Notice Inviting Bids for
  the purchase of a 7-Yard dump truck for the Public Works Division. On April 29, 2021 the
  City Clerk received four bids for the purchase. The bids ranged from $102,972.00 to
  $111,805.00. The bid received from Wondries Fleet Group, in the amount of
  $102,972.00 was the lowest responsible bid. Staff reviewed the bid from Wondries Fleet
  Group and found it is in full compliance and conformance with the bid specifications.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language
  approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, to Wondries Fleet Group in the amount
  of $102,972.00 for the purchase of one 7-yard dump truck; directed the Finance Director
  to appropriate $102,972.00 from the General Fund and appropriate the funding for the
  purchase of this replacement vehicle; and directed staff to undertake the steps
  necessary to finalize Council’s action. (M2M21-60)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

14.  AWARD CONTRACT: WATER QUALITY TESTING LABORATORY SERVICES
  –F2M21-29, RFP2M21-7, C2M21-30, M2M21-61

  On March 8, 2021, the City Council authorized staff to circulate a Request for Proposals
  to qualified companies for water quality testing laboratory services. On April 6, 2021,
  proposals were received from four companies. A review committee comprised of three
  Utilities Department staff members reviewed the four proposals submitted. Staff
  evaluated the proposals based on qualifications, experience, references, technical
  approach, responsiveness and cost. As a result, the review committee agreed that
  Weck Laboratories, Inc. was the most responsive firm.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved a contract, subject to final language
  approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, by and between the City of Alhambra
  and Weck Labs, Inc. for water quality testing laboratory services in an amount not to
  exceed $100,000.00, commencing July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2022, including three,
  one-year extension periods; authorized the City Manager to execute the extensions if the

26.  SECOND READING AND ADOPTION OF AN ORDINANCE ADDING CHAPTER 6.18
  TO THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE FOR MANDATORY ORGANIC WASTE
  DISPOSAL REDUCTION – F2M20-39, O2M21-4787

  In September 2016, Governor Brown signed Senate Bill 1383 (S.B. 1383) also known as
  the Short-Lived Climate Pollutants bill into law. The legislation targeted short-lived
  climate pollutants by focusing on reducing greenhouse gas emissions emitted from
  landfills. This bill established a target diversion rate of 50 percent by 2020 and 75
  percent by 2025 based on 2014 waste characterization levels. The State estimated that
  these reduction targets would result in an annual decrease of at least 4 million metric
  tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. S.B. 1383 sought to accomplish these target
  levels by recycling or diverting organic waste (organics) from being sent to landfills for
  disposal. CalRecycle estimated that two-thirds of the State’s entire waste stream was
  comprised of organic waste. Under S.B. 1383, local jurisdictions must adopt a
  mandatory and enforceable organics waste recycling ordinance. The law mandated that
  jurisdictions were required to provide organics collection and recycling services to all
  residential, both single family and multi-family dwellings, and commercial customers
  within their boundaries. For the purposes of S.B. 1383, organics were not only limited to
  food waste but also included green waste, wood waste, landscape and pruning waste,
  food-soiled paper waste, and fibers such as paper and cardboard. The proposed
  Ordinance was based upon a model ordinance provided by CalRecycle. The ordinance
  would fulfill a major component of S.B. 1383 requirements and would work in concert
  with the City’s new franchise waste hauler agreement to meet the additional provisions
  under State law. Jurisdictions that failed to pass a mandatory organics waste recycling
  ordinance by January 1, 2022, would face compliance actions from the State including
  administrative civil penalties up to $10,000 per day.
  In addition to S.B. 1383 requirements, the proposed Ordinance would also ensure the
  City was in compliance with prior State laws regarding recycling and diversion
  mandates. Prior State legislation includes: A.B. 939 - California Integrated Waste
  Management Act; A.B. 341 - Mandatory Commercial Recycling; A.B. 1594 - Use of
  Green Material as Alternative Daily Cover; A.B. 1826 - Mandatory Commercial Organics
  Recycling and A.B. 827 - Mandatory Commercial Organics Bins. All of these laws
  worked in conjunction to divert as much waste as possible from being landfilled in order
  to offset the effects of climate change by reducing the levels of greenhouse gas
  emissions in California. The proposed ordinance, if approved, would become effective
  July 4, 2021, and would coincide with the commencement of the City’s new franchise

  18
5-24-21
   waste hauler agreement. These two components would work in tandem to ensure the
  City is in compliance with S.B. 1383.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  Declared introduced for its second reading and adopted the
  following ordinance entitled:
  Ordinance No. O2M21-4787: An Ordinance of the City Council of the
  City of Alhambra, California, adding Chapter 6.18 to the Alhambra
  Municipal Code for Mandatory Organic Waste Disposal Reduction
